title: Chapter VIII

teacherSummary.text: At Netherfield the Bingley sisters mock Elizabeth's muddy petticoat. Darcy, Miss Bingley and Elizabeth debate what makes an 'accomplished' woman; Darcy adds 'extensive reading.'

vocabulary.definition: To value, rate, or estimate below the real worth
vocabulary.context: “Eliza Bennet,” said Miss Bingley, when the door was closed on her, “is one of those young ladies who seek to recommend themselves to the other sex, by undervaluing their own; and with many men, I dare say, it succeeds.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “undervalue”: un- (Old English un-, "not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act or process of making nets or network, or of forming meshes, as for fancywork, fishing nets, etc
vocabulary.context: The word is applied to many a woman who deserves it no otherwise than by netting a purse, or covering a screen.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “netting”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Why must she be scampering about the country, because her sister had a cold?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “scamper”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: They solaced their wretchedness, however, by duets after supper, while he could find no better relief to his feelings than by giving his housekeeper directions that every possible attention might be paid to the sick lady and her sister.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “solace”: sol (Latin solus, "alone" / sol, "sun"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: Want of attention, or failure to pay attention
vocabulary.context: Hurst called them to order, with bitter complaints of their inattention to what was going forward.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “inattention”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + ten (Latin tenere, "to hold") + -tion (Latin -tio, "the act of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: Anything that separates or cuts off inconvience, injury, or danger
vocabulary.context: They all paint tables, cover screens and net purses.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “screen”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: A well-known musical instrument somewhat resembling the harpsichord, and consisting of a sreies of wires of…
vocabulary.context: Her performance on the pianoforte is exquisite.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “pianoforte”: fort (Latin fortis, "strong"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: “But it must very materially lessen their chance of marrying men of any consideration in the world,” replied Darcy.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “materially”: -ly (Old English -lice, "in the manner of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To look down upon with disfavor or contempt
vocabulary.context: “Miss Eliza Bennet,” said Miss Bingley, “despises cards.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “despise”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: “Undoubtedly,” replied Darcy, to whom this remark was chiefly addressed, “there is meanness in all the arts which ladies sometimes condescend to employ for captivation.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “condescend”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Female 'accomplishments' (music, drawing, languages) were valued as marriage assets.

significance: Elizabeth's skepticism about impossible standards is a sly critique of how women were judged.
discussionQuestions: What does the debate about accomplishments reveal about each speaker?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with marriage and money?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter VIII,” how does Austen show the accomplished woman? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter VIII, how does Austen develop the idea of the accomplished woman? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter VIII develops the idea of the accomplished woman. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter VIII (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of the accomplished woman. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter VIII suggests about the accomplished woman. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and irony), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter VIII to complicate the reader's understanding of the accomplished woman. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter VIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the accomplished woman responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter VIII alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of the accomplished woman follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter VIII and its treatment of the accomplished woman. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and irony, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter VIII as evidence for a larger claim about the accomplished woman in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter VIII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the accomplished woman. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them
annotationFocus.passage: “Yes, all of them, I think. They all paint tables, cover screens and net purses. I scarcely know anyone who cannot do all this, and I am sure I never heard a young lady spoken of for the first time, without being informed that she was very accomplished.”

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true

annotationFocus.label: Theme
annotationFocus.lookFor: statements or moments that connect to the book's big ideas

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What does the debate about accomplishments reveal about each speaker? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are undervaluing, netting, scampering, solaced, inattention. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: ““Eliza Bennet,” said Miss Bingley, when the door was closed on her, “is one of those young ladies who seek to recommend themselves to the other sex, by undervaluing their own; and with many men, I dare say, it succeeds.” Webster's says: To value, rate, or estimate below the real worth. Now the word history: “undervalue”: un- (Old English un-, "not"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “netting”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it. “scamper”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Female 'accomplishments' (music, drawing, languages) were valued as marriage assets. Why does this chapter matter? Elizabeth's skepticism about impossible standards is a sly critique of how women were judged. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to the accomplished woman.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Irony, Theme.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: “Yes, all of them, I think. They all paint tables, cover screens and net purses. I scarcely know anyone who cannot do all this, and I am sure I never heard a young lady spoken of for the first time, without being informed that she was very accomplished.”

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Irony, Theme: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter VIII,” how does Austen show the accomplished woman? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about the accomplished woman, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes the accomplished woman. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
